clue.text: I rang The Lancet about cure for cold

indicators.note: 'about' can mean in a muddle, all around, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: all fourteen letters taken together

explanation.surface: A caller phones the medical journal to ask about a remedy for the common cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lancet is a famous British medical journal, which pulls the mind towards medicine; the cold here is a chilly house, not an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A system warming a whole building is the remedy for a chilly home, so it cures the cold in a domestic sense.

clue.text: Sentimental stuff, dialogue in old market hall

blocks.note: corn is mawkish, sentimental material
an exchange of words is a dialogue

explanation.surface: Mushy chat taking place inside an old covered market.
explanation.walkthrough: Many British towns have a Victorian building called the Corn Exchange, once used for trading grain.
explanation.definitionFit: A corn exchange was a hall where merchants traded grain, so it is a historic market building.

clue.text: More biting insects initially occupying kid

indicators.note: 'initially' says to keep only the opening letter of the word before it
to occupy is to sit inside something, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a nipper is informal British for a small child
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Insects with a sharper bite are pestering a child.
explanation.walkthrough: A nipper is everyday British slang for a young child.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy describes a cold, sharp, stinging quality, so the comparative form means sharper or more biting.

clue.text: Very exciting ruby stolen

blocks.note: ruby is a shade of red
hot is slang for stolen goods

explanation.surface: A thrilling tale of a stolen ruby.
explanation.definitionFit: Red-hot is an intensifying idiom for something sensational or thrilling, as in red-hot news.

clue.text: Blow a fuse and be deprived of computers etc

blocks.note: to lose something is to be deprived of it
IT, information technology, covers computers and the like

explanation.surface: Someone flies into a rage when the office computers are taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is the same phrase read literally: losing your IT.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose it is an idiom for losing one's temper, exactly like blowing a fuse.

clue.text: Sporting pale scarf to avoid cold, and hat with these?

indicators.note: to avoid something is to leave it out, so one letter is dropped
'sporting' can mean frolicking or playing about, so the letters are set loose and rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Instead of wearing a pale scarf against the chill, choose a hat with these.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a whole: the remaining letters describe the very hat that keeps cold off the ears.
explanation.definitionFit: A hat with these has hanging side pieces covering the ears, so the definition describes the answer by what it belongs to.

clue.text: Note isolated Yankee in social gathering

blocks.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
set apart means isolated
Yankee is Y in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A lone American is noticed standing apart at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea party is an afternoon social occasion where guests meet over tea and cakes.

clue.text: Duck and a trifle

blocks.note: first meaning: a score of zero in cricket
second meaning: something of no importance at all

explanation.surface: A menu of roast duck followed by the sherry-soaked pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batter out without scoring is out for a duck, a nought; trifle is also a British layered pudding, which feeds the dinner picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Zero runs is a score of none, and a mere trifle is a matter of no consequence, both meaning a lack of anything.

clue.text: Secured some fair-trade porridge on the counter

indicators.note: 'some' means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them
counter suggests going the opposite way, as in counter-clockwise, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: letters running across the end of trade and the start of porridge

explanation.surface: Someone buys ethically sourced oats at a shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' paints a shop scene; it is the instruction to read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something roped is tied fast with rope, so it has been secured.

clue.text: Helpers in groups around back of motor vehicle

indicators.note: 'back of' points to the final letter of the word that follows
'around' means one piece encloses the others

blocks.note: sets are groups
last letter of the word
a van is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Assistants are arranged in teams around the rear of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Servants are people employed to help in a household, so they are helpers.

clue.text: Male visiting Henry, poorly outside Surrey, possibly Doctor Foster?

indicators.note: a visitor is a guest staying inside someone's place, so one piece goes into another
'outside' means the first group of letters wraps round the second
'poorly' means unwell or out of shape, so the name's letters are disordered
'possibly' means the county's letters could be arranged another way

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
the name as written
the county as written

explanation.surface: A man visiting a sick Henry in the Home Counties might be a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is an English county south of London. 'Doctor Foster went to Gloucester' is a traditional children's verse; the question mark warns it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Foster is a well-known children's verse, so it is one example of the category.

clue.text: One who trims a head of lettuce, wrapping one piece in paper

indicators.note: 'head of' points to the very first letter of the word that follows
to wrap something is to put it inside a covering, so the outer pieces enclose another

blocks.note: an editor cuts and trims copy
Roman numeral one
taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone trimming a lettuce wraps a portion in newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The trimming and wrapping suggest a greengrocer; the trimmer is someone who cuts text.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is an opinion article written by a newspaper's editor, so it is a piece in a paper.

clue.text: Sadie losing her case near Brussels as I'm leaving

indicators.note: a case is an outer covering, so losing it means dropping the first and last letters

blocks.note: the name as written
Brussels is the seat of the European Union

explanation.surface: Sadie, travelling in Belgium, has her suitcase go missing as she departs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Near' just places the second piece after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is a French farewell, said by someone who is going away for good.

clue.text: Concise crossword usually reasonably tractable at first

indicators.note: 'at first' points to the opening letter of each of the words before it

blocks.note: opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A comment that a crossword tends to be fairly easy to begin with.
explanation.definitionFit: Curt describes speech that is brief to the point of rudeness, so it is a synonym of concise.

clue.text: Betters put on shilling after winning

indicators.note: 'after' sends the pieces before it to follow the piece it governs, so the winning part leads

blocks.note: up means ahead, as in a game
to stage a play is to put it on
s was the abbreviation for a shilling in old British money

explanation.surface: Gamblers place a shilling bet once they are ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Betters' looks like people placing bets; it is the verb meaning outdoes. A shilling was a pre-decimal British coin, abbreviated s.
explanation.definitionFit: To upstage someone is to outshine them and draw attention away, which is to better them.

clue.text: Crate buff or reddish-brown

blocks.note: a chest is a large box
a nut is an enthusiast or buff

explanation.surface: Choosing between paint colours for a crate: buff or reddish-brown.
explanation.walkthrough: Buff looks like another colour beside reddish-brown; it is a fan.
explanation.definitionFit: Chestnut is the deep reddish-brown colour of the nut's shell, used for hair and horses.

clue.text: Might I be shaken after a fall?

definitions.text: Might I be shaken after a fall?

blocks.clueFragment: Might I be shaken after a fall?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone wonders if they will be shocked after tumbling over
setter's reading: an object shaken dry once the rain has fallen

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' suggests a tumble; it means a fall of rain, after which a wet brolly is shaken out.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain shade is opened in a downpour and shaken to dry afterwards, so the clue describes it in the first person.

clue.text: Curse a boring hymn by American

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
an anthem is a hymn or song of praise
A is an abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Someone swears about a tedious hymn by an American composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull; it means drilling into.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is a formal ecclesiastical curse, or more loosely something detested.

clue.text: Sound made by hay fever sufferer is a hoot, surprisingly

definitions.text: Sound made by hay fever sufferer

indicators.note: 'surprisingly' says the letters turn up in an unexpected order

blocks.note: the seven letters as written

explanation.surface: The noise an allergy sufferer makes turns out to be hilarious.
explanation.definitionFit: Atishoo is the British spelling of a sneeze, the noise a pollen allergy provokes.

clue.text: Perjurer's protest retracted

indicators.note: to retract is to draw back, so the word is taken in the backward direction

blocks.note: to rail is to protest angrily

explanation.surface: A witness who lied under oath withdraws their objection.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay; 'retracted' sounds like a courtroom withdrawal.
explanation.definitionFit: A perjurer tells untruths under oath, so is a liar.

clue.text: Baltic officer cutting diamonds in two ways

indicators.note: something cutting into another goes inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: Col is the abbreviation for colonel
ice is slang for diamonds, and D is diamonds in card notation

explanation.surface: A naval officer in the Baltic slices through gems.
explanation.walkthrough: Diamonds are clued twice over: once as slang, once as the card-suit letter, with the officer between them. 'Baltic' is British slang for freezing.
explanation.definitionFit: Baltic is informal British slang for extremely cold weather, after the chilly northern sea.

clue.text: Mark article on church books being covered by copyright

indicators.note: in a down clue 'on' means sitting above the rest, so it comes first
in a down clue being covered means lying beneath, so the later pieces follow the earlier

blocks.note: a is the indefinite article
C is the copyright symbol
CE is the Church of England
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about church books protected by copyright.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent is a mark placed over a letter, such as an acute or grave, to show pronunciation.

clue.text: Take off outside with this old police officer

blocks.note: first meaning: a kitchen tool for removing skin from fruit and vegetables
second meaning: a dated nickname for a policeman, after Sir Robert Peel

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Peel founded London's Metropolitan Police, so early officers were nicknamed after him, as bobbies still are.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen tool strips the skin from a potato, and Victorian slang named constables after Peel.

clue.text: Realises Aga in store is reduced

indicators.note: the phrase is cut down at both ends, leaving only a run of letters from its middle

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A shop is selling off a kitchen range at a discount.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a heavy cast-iron British kitchen stove.
explanation.definitionFit: To realise a sum is to make it as a profit, so realises means gains.

clue.text: Noise and revelry occasionally criminal

indicators.note: 'occasionally' means only now and then, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: a racket is a din
second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Loud partying now and then goes too far.
explanation.definitionFit: A racketeer runs a dishonest or illegal business, so is a criminal.

clue.text: Model Hellenic fabric

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: the word as written

explanation.surface: A Greek-style cloth on display, or a Greek fashion model's fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Chenille is a soft tufted yarn and the velvety cloth woven from it.

clue.text: Potty from lavatory promptly emptied

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its contents, keeping only its first and last letters

blocks.note: loo is British informal for a toilet
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A child's potty is quickly emptied into the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' looks like the child's pot; here it is the adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Potty and loopy are both informal British words for slightly crazy.

clue.text: Cross after draw in game

indicators.note: 'after' places the first-named piece behind the one that follows it in the clue

blocks.note: to contract is to draw together or shrink
to bridge a gap is to cross it

explanation.surface: An angry reaction after a drawn match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective meaning annoyed; it is the verb meaning to span.
explanation.definitionFit: Contract bridge is the standard modern form of the partnership card game played with bidding.
